title: The Smiling Smile
premise: Juniper Hartwell, a pest controller in the dying village of Hollowmere, has spent seven years rationalizing the sounds behind its walls — until the church bell, melted down in 1911, rings again and pulls them into the middle of it. The bell is a mouth, and the village's founding families have been feeding it names for two centuries; whoever learns the song's last verse without singing along can close it forever. As Juniper uncovers their own erased childhood in Hollowmere — they were one of the offered children who escaped — they must race the bell's congregation of the smiling dead to learn the verse from the last woman who refused to sing. In the end Juniper sings the first three verses alone, lets the bell swallow their false name, and rings itself silent, walking out of Hollowmere as someone with no past and, for the first time, a future.
about_author: Orsen Yarrow is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing defunct English village records before turning to horror. They write in unheated rooms and claim to have never once heard a bell they couldn't account for.

chapters.title: Something With Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Called to the Hollowmere chapel to deal with 'scratching,' Juniper finds greasy handprints on the inside of a sealed belfry door — prints too large for any villager, pressed from within. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into recognition: Juniper has seen these prints before, in a dream they've had since childhood.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. At dusk the belfry rings — though parish records confirm the bell was melted down in 1911. Villagers don't flinch; they simply stop mid-sentence and smile toward the sound. Juniper realizes everyone in Hollowmere heard something different. The beat is isolation: the first crack in seven years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Noises
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, intercut with flashbacks. A inventory of every 'explainable' sound Juniper has catalogued since arriving — chewing in walls, humming under floorboards, a lullaby in the well. Each entry now reads like evidence. The beat is dread of self-betrayal: Juniper has been the bell's best cover story.

chapters.title: The Congregation of Smiles
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. At the village meeting about the ringing, Juniper notices everyone over forty smiles identically — same width, same teeth. Old Mrs. Tallow grips Juniper's wrist and whispers, 'Don't learn the last verse.' The beat is creeping paranoia: the whole village may be an audience, or bait.

chapters.title: Records of a Melted Thing
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV at the county archive. The 1911 melting was ordered after eleven children vanished during a harvest song; the bell founder's ledger lists payment for 'one bell, returned.' Juniper finds a faded photograph of the missing children — and their own face among them. The beat is vertigo: memory itself becomes unreliable.

chapters.title: The Name I Gave Away
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, fractured flashbacks. Digging into adoption papers, Juniper recovers fragments: a mother's voice teaching a four-verse song, a father's hand over their mouth on the third verse, running through frost. The beat is grief — Juniper didn't move to Hollowmere; they fled it, and paid for escape with forgetting.

chapters.title: What the Walls Are Chewing
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Investigating the chapel foundations, Juniper finds the walls lined with teeth — human, centuries of them, set like masonry. The scratching isn't pests. Something is being slowly eaten down there, still alive enough to knock. The beat is body-horror revulsion and a terrible new question: who is it?

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow's Third Verse
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tallow's POV. The old woman remembers being nine, singing in the churchyard while her brother was taken mid-line. She has spent seventy years refusing to teach anyone the song, believing ignorance is armor. Now she sees Juniper's face from the photograph and knows the debt has come due. The beat is guilt outlasting a lifetime.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The bell rings at noon and Juniper catches themselves humming harmony they never learned — their feet carrying them toward the chapel against their will. They bite through their own lip to stop. The beat is terror of possession: the song doesn't need consent, only proximity.

chapters.title: The Smiling Man in the Belfry
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper breaks into the belfry and finds no bell — only a vast wet cavity shaped like one, and inside it a figure wearing the face of the man from the melted-down casting, smiling with all the village's identical smiles. It says, 'You left mid-song. We kept your place.' The beat is confrontation with the thing that has been waiting.

chapters.title: Loyalty of the Living
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper begs the vicar and the village elders for help; they refuse gently, lovingly — the bell keeps Hollowmere prosperous, its dead nearby, its griefs audible. Loyalty to the village means feeding it. The beat is betrayal: the true monster is complicity, and it looks like kindness.

chapters.title: The Founder's Daughter
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV in the ruined foundry. Juniper discovers the bell-founder hanged himself in 1912, leaving a letter: he cast his daughter's name into the metal to save her from the offering, and the bell has sung her back ever since. His notes describe the fourth verse — but not its words. The beat is hope with a hole in it.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tallow's POV. She begins teaching Juniper the song in pieces, each verse costing her a memory — she trades her wedding day, then her son's face. The song takes what holds you together. The beat is sacrifice as currency, and Juniper's growing horror at accepting it.

chapters.title: The Knocking Stops
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The thing in the walls goes silent. Juniper digs through the chapel floor and finds a child-sized hollow, warm, empty, shaped recently. Whatever was imprisoned there has been released — or promoted. The beat is dread inverted: silence is worse than noise.

chapters.title: Everyone Knows My Face
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Villagers begin greeting Juniper by their childhood name, Hartwell forgotten. Shopkeepers give them things free. Children sing the third verse outside their window at night. The beat is suffocating belonging — the village is welcoming them home, and home wants to keep them.

chapters.title: Tallow's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Mrs. Tallow is gone; her house smells of bell-metal and her memories are scattered on the floor as small brass tokens. The bell rings her name in her own voice. Juniper understands the price of the final lesson and that they are now the only one left who refuses to smile. The beat is grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Half-Learned
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, dream logic. In sleep, the founder's daughter appears — half girl, half resonance — and teaches Juniper the fourth verse in fragments, warning that hearing it whole means singing it whole. Juniper wakes with most of it, and a tuneless gap where the ending should be. The beat is desperate incompleteness.

chapters.title: Midnight Service
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The entire village gathers in the chapel at midnight, smiling, and begins the song together, pulling Juniper down the aisle by invisible harmony. On the third verse the walls' teeth begin to move. Juniper must hold the fourth verse silently in their mind while their mouth betrays them note by note. The beat is the novel's tightest vise.

chapters.title: Singing Alone
chapters.summary: Climax, Juniper's POV. At the threshold of the belfry-cavity, Juniper does the forbidden thing backwards: sings the first three verses alone, aloud, claiming the song instead of joining it. The bell must answer a singer or lose the song. The dead reach for Juniper's mouth; Mrs. Tallow's brass tokens rise like a shield of remembered things. The beat is terrible courage.

chapters.title: The Verse Without Me
chapters.summary: Climax continued, Juniper's POV. To finish the fourth verse without singing along, Juniper gives the bell a name to take instead — the false self, 'Juniper Hartwell,' seven years of constructed identity. The bell swallows it hungrily. The cavity convulses, the teeth grind to powder, and the bell rings one last time in a child's voice: finished. The beat is annihilation as salvation.

chapters.title: A Village Without a Bell
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, quiet aftermath. Hollowmere wakes ordinary: the elders weep without knowing why, the smiles break into individual faces, and the chapel stands mute. Juniper, nameless now in any record, packs their tools. An old woman who is not quite Mrs. Tallow nods to them across the green. The beat is hollow peace — victory that cost the victor their story.

chapters.title: The Song I Don't Remember
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Juniper's POV. Driving away, Juniper hums something without knowing what it is, and stops. In the rearview mirror, Hollowmere's chapel is simply a chapel. But in the glovebox lies a single brass token, warm, engraved with a name Juniper almost recognizes. The beat is ambiguous grace: some verses are learned so deeply they survive even forgetting.
